paragraphs: Training a neural network requires intermediate results from the forward computation to calculate gradients during backpropagation. Keeping those results consumes memory. Recomputation methods trade some additional calculation for lower memory use: they discard selected intermediate results and reconstruct them when the backward computation needs them.

This paper expresses that tradeoff as a graph problem. Given a fixed memory budget, the objective is to minimize the extra computation caused by discarding results. The authors provide a dynamic programming solution, turning the choice of what to retain and what to recompute into a structured optimization problem. They describe their method as applicable to a wider range of neural networks than earlier approaches.

On the benchmark networks studied, the method reduces peak memory consumption by 36% to 81%, exceeding the reductions achieved by the compared methods. These findings show the practical value of choosing recomputation decisions around the network's computational structure. The benefit concerns peak memory during training, with additional computation forming the central tradeoff.
neurips-2019-a-graph-theoretic-framework.tldr: A graph-based dynamic programming method chooses what to recompute during backpropagation, reducing peak memory by 36% to 81% on tested networks.

paragraphs: Learning recommendation policies through reinforcement learning can require frequent interactions with real users. The paper targets the expense of that process by learning from offline data. It also identifies difficulties with existing offline evaluation approaches: they can require substantial logged data and struggle when the set of possible recommendations is large.

The proposed approach learns a model of interactions between users and the recommendation agent through a generative adversarial network. This model produces interaction sequences that can support policy learning alongside the recorded data. A discriminator evaluates the quality of generated sequences, and its assessments are used to rescale generated rewards. The purpose of this adjustment is to reduce bias in the learned policy.

The authors support the approach with theoretical analysis and empirical evaluations. They report that it identifies patterns in the available offline data and learns effective policies using both offline and generated experience. The contribution connects simulated interaction generation with an explicit mechanism for adjusting how those generated interactions influence policy learning.
neurips-2019-a-model-based-reinforcement.tldr: An adversarially trained interaction model supports offline recommendation policy learning, using discriminator scores to adjust generated rewards and reduce bias.

paragraphs: Graph-based prediction can be vulnerable to adversarial changes in connections or node information. This paper addresses the verification problem: determining whether a prediction is robust to graph perturbations within a specified threat model. Its scope includes a general class of models containing graph neural networks and methods that propagate labels or features.

The authors propose a method for certifying both robustness and non-robustness. Their approach exploits mathematical connections to PageRank and Markov decision processes to make certificate computation efficient. Under many threat models, the certificates can be computed exactly. That qualification matters because the exactness claim depends on the permitted perturbations, rather than applying without distinction to every possible attack setting.

The paper also investigates training procedures designed to improve certified robustness. These procedures increase the number of nodes that can be certified robust while preserving or improving predictive accuracy on clean data. Together, the results connect verification with training: certificates establish which predictions have protection under the threat model, while robust training expands that protected set.
neurips-2019-certifiable-robustness-to-g.tldr: The paper develops efficient robustness certificates for graph-based models and training procedures that increase certified robustness while maintaining or improving clean accuracy.

paragraphs: Code summarization produces a description from code, while code generation proceeds in the opposite direction. Although these tasks are closely related, neural approaches have often trained them separately. This paper asks whether their relationship can become a useful training signal that improves both directions of the mapping.

The authors propose a framework that trains the two tasks simultaneously and explicitly constrains their duality. It introduces regularization terms involving both probabilities and attention weights. These terms encourage consistency between the two tasks at the level of their predictions and attention, making their relationship part of the learning objective rather than merely sharing a broad application area.

Experiments on two datasets collected from GitHub show improvements over baselines for both code summarization and code generation. The findings support using the reverse task as an additional source of structure during training. The stated result is an empirical improvement in both tasks on the evaluated datasets; it does not establish that the two learned mappings perfectly reverse one another.
neurips-2019-code-generation-as-a-dual-t.tldr: Joint training that constrains the dual relationship between code generation and summarization improves both tasks on two GitHub-derived datasets.

paragraphs: Graph embedding converts a network's discrete structure into a vector representation. This paper studies the reverse direction: generating graph structures from related semantic context. The motivating idea is that a graph becomes more meaningful when connected to a condition, such as a particular community for a social network or a disease for a gene network.

The authors formulate this as conditional structure generation and introduce CondGen, a unified graph variational generative adversarial model. It addresses two central challenges: flexibly relating semantic context to graph structure, and producing graphs in a permutation-invariant way. The latter means that the generation problem must respect graph structure without attaching significance to an arbitrary ordering of nodes.

The evaluation uses two deliberately constructed benchmark datasets containing real-world networks enriched with context. The authors report strong effectiveness and generalizability on these benchmarks. The contribution therefore extends graph generation toward structures guided by supplied meaning, with experiments supporting the model's ability to handle the relationship between context and network form.
neurips-2019-conditional-structure-gener.tldr: CondGen generates graph structures conditioned on semantic context while addressing flexible context relationships and permutation-invariant generation.

paragraphs: Sparse depth completion fills in missing distance measurements using the depth values that are available and information from a color image. The paper introduces CFCNet, an end-to-end model that learns how RGB and depth information relate. Its central idea is to capture shared semantic features so that one source can help reconstruct missing information in the other.

Training uses image pixels paired with visible measurements in a sparse depth map to learn transformations between the two feature representations. For a location without a depth measurement, the model can transform the corresponding RGB features into predicted depth features and reconstruct depth from them. The authors extend canonical correlation analysis into a two-dimensional formulation and use it as a training objective to encourage this relationship.

Experiments cover indoor and outdoor scenes with different real-life patterns of sparse measurements. The authors report that these evaluations validate CFCNet's capabilities and flexibility relative to state-of-the-art methods. The approach makes the learned relationship between color and depth an explicit part of completion.
neurips-2019-deep-rgb-d-canonical-correl.tldr: CFCNet learns correlated RGB and depth features to reconstruct missing depth, using a two-dimensional canonical correlation training objective.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to identify a nearly best option when trying different options has unequal costs. In its Pay-Per-Reward setting, the cost of exploring an arm is proportional to that arm's expected future reward. The objective is to return an arm whose expected reward lies within epsilon of the best available one.

The authors give an algorithm with a high-probability guarantee of finding such an arm. Its exploration cost depends only linearly on the sum of expected rewards across all arms, with no separate dependence on the number of arms. This shifts the cost characterization from counting available choices to measuring their combined expected reward under the specified payment rule.

That distinction does not imply that adding arms can never change the cost: additional arms can change the total expected reward. The result instead removes arm count as an independent factor in the stated bound. Under mild assumptions, the authors also extend the algorithm's applicability to problems with infinitely many arms, broadening the setting beyond a finite list of choices.
neurips-2019-epsilon-best-arm-identifica.tldr: A Pay-Per-Reward bandit algorithm identifies an epsilon-best arm with high probability at a cost linear in total expected reward, without separate arm-count dependence.

paragraphs: Recovering relationships among many variables is difficult when observations are scarce. The paper targets graphical structure learning in this setting, where existing methods can be computationally expensive and may impose unsuitable sparsity assumptions. It proposes a different structural preference: modules in which each observed variable has a single latent parent.

The method derives its optimization objective from a connection between information-theoretic measures and structured latent factor models. The objective encourages this modular organization, and each optimization step has computational cost linear in the number of observed variables. This makes the proposed approach relevant to settings where the number of variables itself is a major computational obstacle.

In synthetic experiments, the method is the only evaluated approach whose modular structure recovery improves as dimensionality increases. On real-world covariance estimation datasets, it consistently outperforms the compared state-of-the-art estimators at substantially lower computational cost. An application to high-resolution fMRI data with more than 100,000 voxels also extracts meaningful patterns, demonstrating the method's use at a large observational scale.
neurips-2019-fast-structure-learning-wit.tldr: An information-theoretic objective encourages modular latent structure, enabling linear-cost optimization steps and strong empirical covariance estimation performance.

paragraphs: Some reinforcement learning algorithms involve two coupled learning processes operating on different time scales. This paper studies linear stochastic approximation models of that kind, which can represent algorithms including GTD, GTD2, and TDC. Its focus is performance after a finite amount of learning, rather than only behavior after indefinitely many updates.

The authors derive finite-time performance bounds when the learning rate is fixed. Their main analytical tool is a Lyapunov function motivated by singular perturbation theory for linear differential equations. This provides a way to analyze the coupled dynamics and turn that analysis into bounds relevant to the learning process.

The resulting bound also guides an adaptive learning rate scheme. In experiments, this scheme substantially improves convergence over the known optimal polynomial decay rule. The authors further describe potential improvements to other schedules that change learning rates at predetermined times. The distinction is important: the fixed-rate bounds are theoretical results, while the reported adaptive advantage is experimental and the broader scheduling benefit is presented as a possibility.
neurips-2019-finite-time-performance-bou.tldr: Finite-time bounds for two-time-scale learning motivate an adaptive learning rate scheme that improves convergence over polynomial decay in experiments.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning policy can fit its training environments closely yet perform poorly in new ones. Regularization offers a way to address that problem, but techniques developed for supervised learning do not transfer without complications. This paper examines those differences, focusing on methods that inject noise into the learned function, including dropout and batch normalization.

The authors propose Selective Noise Injection, or SNI, to preserve the regularizing benefits of noise while reducing its harmful effects on gradient quality. The key concern is that a technique intended to improve generalization can also interfere with the signal used to learn a policy. SNI aims to manage both effects within the reinforcement learning setting.

The paper also finds the Information Bottleneck particularly suitable for the low-data conditions encountered early in reinforcement learning. Combining it with SNI significantly outperforms the reported state of the art, including on Coinrun. These results support adapting regularization to the learning process itself, with attention to both limited early experience and the quality of policy updates.
neurips-2019-generalization-in-reinforce.tldr: Selective Noise Injection combined with an Information Bottleneck improves reinforcement learning generalization while mitigating noise-related degradation of gradient quality.

paragraphs: An online continual learner receives a changing stream of data and must avoid forgetting what it learned earlier. A replay buffer helps by retaining old examples for rehearsal, but its contents must be chosen carefully. The paper addresses selection in a setting where earlier approaches often depend on task boundaries or assumptions that examples are independent and identically distributed.

The authors formulate buffer selection through constrained optimization. Previous examples define constraints on learning, and the goal is to retain a fixed subset that approximates the feasible region defined by the full collection. They show that this formulation is equivalent to maximizing diversity when each example is represented by its gradient with respect to the model parameters.

This gives sample diversity a learning-specific meaning: examples are compared through how they affect parameter updates. The paper also develops a cheap, efficient greedy alternative. Experiments demonstrate advantages over other selection approaches, and comparisons with state-of-the-art methods that rely on task boundaries yield comparable or better results for the proposed method.
neurips-2019-gradient-based-sample-selec.tldr: Selecting replay examples for diverse parameter gradients approximates continual learning constraints and achieves competitive results without relying on task boundaries.

paragraphs: To distinguish two distributions from samples, a standard approach searches for a function whose average output differs between them. This paper asks whether a discriminator gains expressive power by examining several examples together. The question is relevant to settings such as generative adversarial networks, where real and generated distributions must be distinguished.

The authors define discriminators built from Boolean functions of k examples. Each function can be interpreted as describing whether a hyperedge exists among those examples. Discrimination depends on a difference in the function's expected output on independently sampled tuples from the two distributions. The familiar single-example formulation appears as the special case k equals one.

The theoretical results establish an expressiveness separation between functions acting on k examples and those acting on k plus one. They also introduce an analogue of VC dimension for these function families when k is at least two. Upper and lower bounds show how this quantity controls sample complexity, connecting the extra expressive capability to the amount of data needed.
neurips-2019-graph-based-discriminators-.tldr: Discriminators that inspect tuples of examples have provably different expressive power, with sample complexity governed by an extended VC-dimension notion.

paragraphs: Aligning related datasets means finding a transformation that makes their contents meaningfully correspond. Optimal transport approaches express this through distribution matching. This paper introduces a hierarchical formulation that uses clusters within the data to improve alignment when the distributions are noisy, ambiguous, or contain several distinct modes.

The numerical method combines distributed ADMM with the Sinkhorn distance, with computational complexity scaling quadratically in the size of the largest cluster. The paper also gives performance guarantees for recovering cluster correspondences when the transformation between datasets is unitary. It examines both favorable recovery conditions and worst-case dataset geometry, making the geometric assumptions part of the analysis.

Experiments study mixtures of low-rank Gaussians and a neural decoding application involving movement directions and instantaneous velocities from macaque motor cortex activity. The results show that exploiting clusters can substantially improve cross-domain alignment when those clusters exist and remain consistent across trials or time points. That consistency is central to the stated benefit: the hierarchy supplies useful correspondence information when the datasets share its structure.
neurips-2019-hierarchical-optimal-transp.tldr: Hierarchical optimal transport improves alignment by exploiting consistent cluster structure, with conditional recovery guarantees and evidence from synthetic and neural datasets.

paragraphs: A network's initial parameter values affect whether information remains usable as it passes through many layers. This paper focuses on weight-normalized networks, including those with residual connections. It argues that initialization methods borrowed from unnormalized networks overlook relevant structure, while simplified analyses of residual networks can ignore their shortcut connections.

The authors develop an initialization strategy using a theoretical analysis based on a mean field approximation. The strategy is designed to prevent information from exploding or vanishing across layers in weight-normalized networks with and without residual connections. Accounting for these architectural features makes the initialization directly responsive to the networks being trained.

Across more than 2,500 experiments on image datasets, the proposed method improves generalization, robustness to hyperparameter choices, and variation across random seeds relative to existing initializations. The advantage is especially pronounced for deeper networks, where existing methods can fail to begin training. Combining the initialization with learning rate warmup also narrows the performance gap between weight-normalized and batch-normalized networks, without a claim that it eliminates that gap.
neurips-2019-how-to-initialize-your-netw.tldr: A mean-field-based initialization stabilizes information flow in weight-normalized networks and improves training robustness, particularly as networks become deeper.

paragraphs: Model-agnostic meta-learning seeks parameters that can adapt to a new task after a few gradient updates. A shared initialization works toward that goal across related tasks, but a single starting point can restrict the diversity of tasks the method handles. This paper considers task distributions containing multiple modes, or different groups of task characteristics.

The proposed MMAML framework augments MAML by identifying the mode of a sampled task and modulating its meta-learned prior parameters accordingly. Gradient-based adaptation then proceeds from that adjusted starting point. The mechanism separates recognizing what kind of task is present from the subsequent rapid parameter updates, allowing the initial parameters to respond to task characteristics.

Evaluations cover few-shot regression, image classification, and reinforcement learning. The results support the effectiveness of the modulation mechanism and show that training across a multimodal task distribution can improve performance over unimodal training. This is an empirical possibility demonstrated by the study, rather than a guarantee that increasing task diversity always improves adaptation.
neurips-2019-multimodal-model-agnostic-m.tldr: MMAML adjusts meta-learned starting parameters to a task's identified mode, enabling effective few-shot adaptation across diverse task distributions.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to produce a sparse representation of a graph while ensuring differential privacy. The output graph approximates the spectrum of the original graph, retaining a mathematical description of its structure in a form with fewer edges. The goal is to make useful graph computations both private and computationally efficient.

The sparsification algorithm serves as a general method that can support several downstream graph problems. Its value comes from combining privacy with structural approximation: the sparse graph is intended to preserve information useful for later computations while satisfying the privacy requirement. The paper demonstrates this role through methods for privately answering cut queries and practical algorithms for MAX-CUT and SPARSEST-CUT.

For the cut optimization applications, the authors report better accuracy than previously known private approaches. They also provide what they describe as the first efficient private algorithm for learning a Laplacian eigenmap on a graph. These applications show that the contribution extends beyond producing a smaller graph to enabling a range of private structural analyses.
neurips-2019-on-differentially-private-g.tldr: Private spectral graph sparsification enables efficient graph analysis, including improved private cut algorithms and an efficient private Laplacian eigenmap algorithm.

paragraphs: Nesterov's accelerated gradient method is the subject of this paper's geometric interpretation. For strongly convex problems, the authors view optimization as taking place on a Riemannian manifold, a space equipped with a geometry that can be curved. The aim is to explain the accelerated update through that geometry.

In this formulation, the accelerated method can be understood as a proximal point method applied in the curved space. This connects two optimization procedures by changing the geometric setting in which the updates are interpreted. The contribution is therefore a mathematical explanation of acceleration, with the manifold's natural structure playing a central role in the correspondence.

The perspective also extends to continuous time through an ordinary differential equation on the manifold. A natural block-implicit Euler discretization of that equation gives rise to the accelerated gradient method. The authors analyze the equation's convergence rate for quadratic objectives. This scope distinguishes the broader strongly convex motivation from the particular class of objectives covered by the stated continuous-time convergence analysis.
neurips-2019-on-the-curved-geometry-of-a.tldr: The paper interprets Nesterov acceleration as a proximal point method on a curved manifold and analyzes related continuous-time dynamics for quadratic objectives.

paragraphs: The paper examines how prediction error changes as a regression model uses more features. It assumes uncorrelated Gaussian features selected from highest to lowest variance. When the selected feature count does not exceed the number of observations, the estimator coincides with principal component regression. Beyond that point, it uses the solution with the smallest Euclidean norm.

The analysis considers average prediction error on new data as the total feature count, selected feature count, and sample size all grow. The proportions of selected features and observations relative to the total feature count approach fixed constants. This gives a defined large-scale setting for comparing models on both sides of the point where features outnumber observations.

Within this setting, the prediction error follows a double descent shape as the number of selected features changes. The authors also establish conditions under which the lowest risk occurs in the interpolating regime, where selected features exceed observations. The result shows that this regime can be optimal under the analyzed conditions, rather than asserting that it is always preferable.
neurips-2019-on-the-number-of-variables-.tldr: An average-case analysis of Gaussian-feature regression finds double descent and conditions where using more features than observations minimizes prediction risk.

paragraphs: The paper studies visual political bias through how news sources portray subjects and topics. It assembles more than one million unique images and their associated articles from left- and right-leaning sources. The prediction problem is challenging because images associated with the same political leaning can differ greatly in both appearance and meaning.

The proposed method learns in two stages. First, a model learns relevant visual concepts together with document embeddings from the articles paired with the images, using both to predict bias. Second, the authors train a visual classifier from the first model's features, removing the need for accompanying text. Article information thus helps shape the visual representation during learning.

The authors report that this two-stage process makes learning easier and outperforms several strong baselines. They also provide qualitative results illustrating nuances in the data. The findings support using paired image and article information to learn visual associations with political leaning in news media, with the final classification stage operating on images without requiring the text domain.
neurips-2019-predicting-the-politics-of-.tldr: A two-stage method uses paired news articles to learn visual features for predicting political leaning, then classifies images without accompanying text.

paragraphs: Sampling from a posterior distribution becomes difficult when it contains several separated modes. A Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler can spend many iterations trapped around one mode, delaying exploration of the others. This paper introduces pseudo-extended MCMC to improve movement between these separated regions and thereby improve mixing.

The method enlarges the posterior's state space by introducing pseudo-samples as auxiliary variables. In the extended space, the posterior modes become connected, allowing the sampler to move more easily between regions that were well separated in the original representation. The central intervention is therefore in the space being explored, using additional variables to change how the modes connect.

The authors demonstrate improved sampling compared with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo on multimodal posterior problems. Their examples include Boltzmann machines and models with priors that encourage sparsity. These results support the usefulness of the extended representation for difficult multimodal sampling. The reported advantage concerns the evaluated posterior settings, while the mechanism specifically targets the difficulty of moving between separated modes.
neurips-2019-pseudo-extended-markov-chai.tldr: Pseudo-extended MCMC adds auxiliary pseudo-samples to connect posterior modes and improves sampling over Hamiltonian Monte Carlo in the evaluated multimodal settings.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor classification becomes harder to organize when a dataset cannot reside on one machine because of computational, communication, privacy, or ownership constraints. The paper studies a divide-and-conquer approach called bigNN. Each smaller data partition produces a nearest-neighbor prediction, and majority voting combines those predictions into a final classification.

The authors establish convergence rates for both excess risk and classification instability under minimal assumptions. These rates match those of an oracle nearest-neighbor classifier and are shown to be unimprovable in the analyzed setting. They also study a pre-training acceleration technique that substantially reduces the prediction time needed to achieve the optimal rate, with a convergence guarantee of its own.

The analysis identifies a coordination requirement across partitions: the best choice of neighbor count depends on both the total sample size and the number of partitions. It also establishes a theoretical upper limit on partition count. Numerical studies verify the theoretical findings, supporting distributed classification while showing that partitioning and local neighbor selection must be chosen together.
neurips-2019-rates-of-convergence-for-la.tldr: Distributed nearest-neighbor voting achieves optimal convergence rates under the analyzed assumptions, with theory guiding partition counts, neighbor selection, and prediction acceleration.

paragraphs: Training with softmax cross entropy becomes expensive as the number of classes grows. Sampled softmax reduces work by estimating the gradient from a subset of classes. However, the estimate is biased unless classes are sampled from the exact softmax distribution, and computing that distribution recreates the expense that sampling is intended to avoid.

This paper analyzes how the choice of sampling distribution affects the quality of sampled softmax. Guided by that analysis and kernel-based sampling, the authors introduce Random Fourier Softmax. It uses Random Fourier Features to sample efficiently from an approximation to the softmax distribution, aiming to improve the sampling quality without paying for the full distribution.

The authors show low estimation bias relative to both the full softmax distribution and its gradient. They also report that the method's cost scales logarithmically with the number of classes. The contribution links computational savings with an analysis of approximation quality: the proposed sampler seeks a more faithful learning signal while preserving the speed advantage of sampling.
neurips-2019-sampled-softmax-with-random.tldr: Random Fourier Softmax provides low-bias approximate softmax sampling with cost that scales logarithmically in the number of classes.

paragraphs: Capsule networks organize each layer into capsules that specialize in different regions of feature space. Traditional routing by agreement coordinates connections between neighboring layers and can filter noisy capsule predictions. This paper identifies two drawbacks of that process: substantial computation and a clustering assumption that may break down under heavy input noise.

The authors replace agreement-based coordination with self-routing. Each capsule uses its own subordinate routing network to determine its routing independently. Upper-layer capsule poses and activations are then obtained through a mechanism similar to a mixture of experts. This removes the requirement for capsules to agree with one another before establishing their influence on the next layer.

Experiments on CIFAR-10, SVHN, and SmallNORB show greater robustness to white-box adversarial attacks and affine transformations while requiring less computation. The findings indicate that the simpler routing mechanism can improve both efficiency and empirical robustness in the tested settings. They also support reconsidering whether agreement-based clustering is necessary to obtain useful capsule behavior.
neurips-2019-self-routing-capsule-networ.tldr: Self-routing lets capsules route independently, reducing computation and improving robustness to tested adversarial attacks and affine transformations.

paragraphs: The paper studies finding an input to a deep network whose output matches a target, measured by squared error. Optimizing this objective on a fully trained network can be difficult because its surface is nonconvex. The proposed surfing procedure instead follows a sequence of objectives defined by network parameters from successive stages of training.

For the network families considered, the authors show that the objective at random initialization is easy to optimize with gradient descent. As training progresses, small parameter changes make the objective surface evolve gradually. Surfing incrementally updates the input solution along this evolution, carrying it from the initial landscape toward the final learned one.

The algorithm is formalized and analyzed for a family of expansive networks. Experiments demonstrate cases where surfing finds the global optimum and succeeds in compressed sensing even when direct gradient descent on the final network fails. These findings support using the training trajectory as an optimization resource, with the theoretical analysis tied to the specified network family.
neurips-2019-surfing-iterative-optimizat.tldr: Surfing optimizes an input across successive network training stages, succeeding in experiments where direct optimization of the final network fails.

paragraphs: Speech recognition networks perform well, but their internal treatment of sound is less understood than the operation of many vision models. This paper investigates how speech information changes across network layers. It uses a statistical mechanical theory linking the geometry of internal representations to how easily different classes can be separated.

The analysis finds that the network hierarchy discards speaker-specific variation that is irrelevant to recognition, while later layers make words and phonemes more separable. Higher-level properties, including parts of speech and context dependence, also emerge in later layers. These observations describe a progression in which representations increasingly organize information around the recognition task.

The paper additionally examines the temporal dimension of speech processing. It finds substantial temporal untangling, with deep representations efficiently extracting task-relevant features at each computation step. Together, the findings explain aspects of invariant recognition: the studied networks reduce nuisance variation while reorganizing useful linguistic and time-dependent information. The contribution is an account of observed internal processing, connecting representation geometry to the emergence of recognizable concepts.
neurips-2019-untangling-in-invariant-spe.tldr: A geometric analysis finds that speech networks discard speaker-specific nuisance variation while separating linguistic concepts and extracting relevant temporal features.
